# Lecture roadmaps

*Generated by `tools/textbook/teaching_docs.js` from `tools/concepts/assessments.json`, `bridges.json` and the registry: do not edit by hand.*

For each lecture: what it builds on, today's outcomes, the learning status of its concepts, the bridges that recall what was deferred, the next step and the closing thread. The same text opens the notes of each deck and the chapter of the textbook.

## Lecture 00: Course Introduction

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) describe the four steps of the learning spiral and say why a prediction comes before running; (2) state the assessment rules: one midterm, two exam parts that must both be passed, no devices and no AI. Builds on: nothing: it is the first lecture. Next: Lecture 01, PRG32 and PRG32-QT: Setting Up Your Workshop.

Closing thread: The course runs on one method: play, observe, formalise, return. Every topic will start as something seen on PRG32 and end as a rule that lets you predict it. Next: installing the workshop.

**Learning status.** Learning status of this lecture. UNDERSTAND NOW: the program-first method; the rules of the course. USE NOW: the complete program, the PRG32 tools (used, not studied, in this course). UNDERSTAND LATER: the pieces of PRG32 (Lecture 01); RISC and an open ISA (Lecture 03); the Verm1 project (Lecture 07). A slide without a badge is context: a story, an example, a question, an exercise.

## Lecture 01: PRG32 and PRG32-QT: Setting Up Your Workshop

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) explain the path from a source file to a running cartridge: source, translator, machine code, cartridge, host; (2) run a cartridge in PRG32-QT and build one with the terminal. Builds on: Lecture 00, and Starting from Zero for a reader who has never programmed. Next: Lecture 02, First Contact: RISC-V Assembly on PRG32.

Closing thread: You now own the whole cycle: write a source file, translate it, send the cartridge to a host, stop it in the debugger. Next: writing the source file yourself.

**Learning status.** Learning status of this lecture. UNDERSTAND NOW: program, source and machine code; the pieces of PRG32. USE NOW: the terminal, the PRG32 tools, the PRG32-QT debugger, the complete program (used, not studied, in this course). UNDERSTAND LATER: the init, update, draw contract (Lecture 02); registers (Lecture 02). A slide without a badge is context: a story, an example, a question, an exercise.

## Lecture 02: First Contact: RISC-V Assembly on PRG32

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) build and run a cartridge, and say when the runtime calls init, update and draw; (2) read a line of assembly: label, instruction, operands, comment; (3) tell an address from a value, and trace what la, lw, addi and sw leave in registers and memory. Builds on: only what Lecture 01 set up. Next: Lecture 03, History of Computing.

Closing thread: A program is a few functions that the runtime calls; each line is one instruction; values live in registers while they are computed and in memory between frames. Everything else you used today has a lecture of its own. Next: where these ideas came from.

**Learning status.** Learning status of this lecture. UNDERSTAND NOW: registers, compute, move, jump; registers; functions, call and return; the init, update, draw contract; reading a line of assembly; arguments in a0 to a7; why ra is saved; address, value, load, store; the base instructions; pseudo-instructions; an instruction is a number; tracing by hand. USE NOW: hexadecimal (Lecture 04); bit, byte, word (Lecture 04); the calling convention (Lecture 18); bit masks (Lecture 08) and, used without being studied in this course, the assembler directives, the PRG32 tools, the PRG32 runtime calls, the PRG32-QT debugger, the complete program. UNDERSTAND LATER: the stack (Lecture 18); addressing modes (Lecture 19); instruction formats (Lecture 19); two's complement (Lecture 05); fixed point (Lecture 06); Boolean algebra (Lecture 08); the adder (Lecture 09); from volts to bits (Lecture 10); latches and flip-flops (Lecture 13); the processor cycle (Lecture 19); the Verm1 project (Lecture 07). A slide without a badge is context: a story, an example, a question, an exercise.

## Lecture 03: History of Computing

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) define informatics and explain why it is not only about computers; (2) name the units of the von Neumann architecture and its stored-program idea; (3) say what distinguishes RISC from CISC and why RISC-V is open. Builds on: only what Lecture 01 set up. Next: Lecture 04, Representing Digital Information.

Closing thread: The machine you programmed in Lecture 02 is a von Neumann machine: program and data in one memory. RISC-V is the latest step of a long debate on how simple instructions should be. Next: how anything at all becomes bits.

**Learning status.** Learning status of this lecture. UNDERSTAND NOW: what informatics is; the von Neumann architecture; RISC and an open ISA. USE NOW: the complete program, the PRG32 tools (used, not studied, in this course). UNDERSTAND LATER: Boolean algebra (Lecture 08). A slide without a badge is context: a story, an example, a question, an exercise.

## Lecture 04: Representing Digital Information

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) distinguish analog from digital information and count the values that n bits can represent; (2) encode numbers, colours and text as bits: positional notation, hexadecimal, RGB565, ASCII; (3) name the basic data structures and the properties of an algorithm. Builds on: only what Lecture 01 set up. Next: Lecture 05, Number Representation: Integers.

Bridge. In Lecture 02 the instruction addi t1, t1, 1 appeared in memory as the word 0x00130313. Today the same 32 bits can be read as a number, a colour, four letters or an instruction: the code decides. Lecture 19 reads the instruction field by field. Recall: Name two different things one 32-bit word can mean, and what decides which meaning applies.

Closing thread: Bits mean nothing by themselves: a code gives them a meaning, and the same 32 bits can be a number, a colour, four letters or an instruction. Next: the codes for integers, and what happens when they run out of bits.

**Learning status.** Learning status of this lecture. UNDERSTAND NOW: analog and digital; bit, byte, word; hexadecimal; positional notation; a colour is a number; characters and strings; little-endian byte order; data structures; arrays in memory; algorithms. USE NOW: shifts as multiplications (Lecture 05) and, used without being studied in this course, the complete program, the PRG32 tools. UNDERSTAND LATER: nothing. A slide without a badge is context: a story, an example, a question, an exercise.

## Lecture 05: Number Representation: Integers

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) convert between bases and read an n-bit pattern as unsigned and as two's complement; (2) recognise overflow in unsigned and in signed addition; (3) choose between signed and unsigned instructions, including lb and lbu. Builds on: only what Lecture 01 set up. Next: Lecture 06, Number Representation: Real Numbers.

Closing thread: The 0xFFFFFFFF of a counter that went below zero is -1 in two's complement: the bits did not change, the reading did. Next: fractions on a chip with no floating-point unit.

**Learning status.** Learning status of this lecture. UNDERSTAND NOW: two's complement; base conversions; naturals and overflow; shifts as multiplications; sign and magnitude; signed or unsigned instructions; sign extension. USE NOW: the PRG32 runtime calls, the complete program, the PRG32 tools (used, not studied, in this course). UNDERSTAND LATER: nothing. A slide without a badge is context: a story, an example, a question, an exercise.

## Lecture 06: Number Representation: Real Numbers

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) represent a real number in fixed point and compute with it using integer instructions; (2) decode an IEEE 754 single-precision number; (3) read the name RV32IMAC and say what the kit can and cannot compute in hardware. Builds on: only what Lecture 01 set up. Next: Lecture 07, Verm1, Part 1: A Head That Crosses the World.

Closing thread: Without an F extension, fractions are integers with an agreed scale: Verm1 will move its head by fractions of a cell exactly this way. Next: the first part of the project.

**Learning status.** Learning status of this lecture. UNDERSTAND NOW: fixed point; one's complement and excess-k; IEEE 754 floating point; the name RV32IMAC. USE NOW: the complete program, the PRG32 tools (used, not studied, in this course). UNDERSTAND LATER: nothing. A slide without a badge is context: a story, an example, a question, an exercise.

## Lecture 07: Verm1, Part 1: A Head That Crosses the World

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) build a cartridge from an empty file: a grid, a title and a moving head; (2) place constants and variables in the right section, .rodata or .data; (3) control a speed with a fixed-point accumulator. Builds on: the init, update, draw contract (Lecture 02); a colour is a number (Lecture 04); arrays in memory (Lecture 04); address, value, load, store (Lecture 02); why ra is saved (Lecture 02). Next: Lecture 08, Elements of Boolean Algebra.

Bridge. In Lecture 02 step 2 saved ra on the stack before its calls, and lw t1, 0(t0) read a word at the address in t0. Today verm1_draw saves ra and verm1_update does not, and every variable of Verm1 is read with la and lw. Lecture 18 explains the stack and the calling convention; Lecture 19 names the addressing modes. Recall: Why does verm1_draw save ra while verm1_update does not?

Closing thread: Numbers became positions, colours and a speed: the whole information block, in one running game. Next: the logic that will let the player steer it.

**Learning status.** Learning status of this lecture. UNDERSTAND NOW: the Verm1 project; the init, update, draw contract; a colour is a number; arrays in memory; .text, .rodata, .data; address, value, load, store; why ra is saved; shifts as multiplications; fixed point; pseudo-instructions; little-endian byte order. USE NOW: the PRG32 tools, the PRG32-QT debugger (used, not studied, in this course). UNDERSTAND LATER: instruction formats (Lecture 19). ## Lecture 08: Elements of Boolean Algebra

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) tell the analysis of a logic circuit from its synthesis; (2) apply the axioms and theorems of Boolean algebra, De Morgan's included; (3) set, clear and test bits with masks. Builds on: the von Neumann architecture (Lecture 03). Next: Lecture 09, Elements of Boolean Algebra.

Closing thread: andi t3, t0, 1 is a row of 32 AND gates: Boolean algebra describes both the instruction and the circuit. Next: from a truth table to the smallest circuit.

**Learning status.** Learning status of this lecture. UNDERSTAND NOW: bit masks; the von Neumann architecture; analysis and synthesis; Boolean algebra; logic gates. USE NOW: the complete program, the PRG32 tools (used, not studied, in this course). UNDERSTAND LATER: minimisation, Karnaugh maps (Lecture 09). A slide without a badge is context: a story, an example, a question, an exercise.

## Lecture 09: Elements of Boolean Algebra

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) write a function in canonical form from its truth table; (2) minimise a function of up to four variables with a Karnaugh map; (3) build a full adder and chain it into an n-bit adder. Builds on: only what Lecture 01 set up. Next: Lecture 10, Introduction to Electronics and Digital Electronics.

Closing thread: The add of Lecture 02 is now a circuit you could draw: 32 full adders and a carry that ripples. Next: the electronics that make a gate.

## Lecture 10: Introduction to Electronics and Digital Electronics

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) explain how a MOS transistor works as a switch and how CMOS builds a gate; (2) read logic levels and noise margins from voltages; (3) size the resistor of an LED and explain the pull-up of a button. Builds on: only what Lecture 01 set up. Next: Lecture 11, Combinational Machines.

Bridge. In Lecture 02 the counter survived from one frame to the next in memory, not in a register. Today a memory cell costs about 6 transistors and a flip-flop about 20: remembering a bit is a circuit. Lecture 13 shows how latches and flip-flops keep a bit. Recall: Where did the counter of Lecture 02 live between two frames, and why not in t1?

Closing thread: A bit is a voltage inside a guaranteed range, and a gate is a few switches: the button of the kit is now a circuit you understand. Next: the machines built from gates.

**Learning status.** Learning status of this lecture. UNDERSTAND NOW: pull-up inputs; voltage, current, Ohm's law; the transistor as a switch; from volts to bits; CMOS gates. USE NOW: the complete program, the PRG32 tools (used, not studied, in this course). UNDERSTAND LATER: the clock (Lecture 13). A slide without a badge is context: a story, an example, a question, an exercise.

## Lecture 11: Combinational Machines

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) tell a combinational machine from a sequential one; (2) use decoders, multiplexers, comparators and parity; (3) explain the ALU as parallel units and a multiplexer. Builds on: only what Lecture 01 set up. Next: Lecture 12, Verm1, Part 2: Steering, Food and a Score.

Bridge. In Lecture 02 an instruction was a 32-bit number, and the processor somehow knew what to do with it. Today a decoder reads a field of that number, funct3, and drives the multiplexer that picks the ALU's result. Lecture 19 describes all the fields and the fetch, decode, execute cycle. Recall: Which part of the word of an instruction tells the ALU to add rather than to compute an AND?

Closing thread: The ALU that executed every add so far is one large combinational machine: many results computed at once, one chosen. Next: these circuits at work in the second part of Verm1.

**Learning status.** Learning status of this lecture. UNDERSTAND NOW: multiplexers; combinational machines; codes; decoders and encoders; comparators and parity; the ALU. USE NOW: the complete program, the PRG32 tools (used, not studied, in this course). UNDERSTAND LATER: finite-state machines (Lecture 13). A slide without a badge is context: a story, an example, a question, an exercise.

## Lecture 12: Verm1, Part 2: Steering, Food and a Score

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) read the buttons with masks and refuse a U-turn with one XOR; (2) compare positions with XOR and OR to detect food; (3) keep and show a score. Builds on: bit masks (Lecture 08); codes (Lecture 11); arrays in memory (Lecture 04); pull-up inputs (Lecture 10); Boolean algebra (Lecture 08). Next: Lecture 13, Sequential Machines.

Bridge. In Lecture 07 a function that calls another saved ra in a frame of 16 bytes. Today the functions of Verm1 call each other more deeply: each saves ra once, on entry, and restores it before ret. Lecture 18 states the rules: which registers a call may change and which it must preserve. Recall: A function calls two other functions. How many times must it save ra, and where?

Closing thread: Every rule of the game became a few logic instructions: a mask, an XOR, a comparison. Next: circuits that remember, and the states of a game.

**Learning status.** Learning status of this lecture. UNDERSTAND NOW: bit masks; codes; arrays in memory; pull-up inputs; Boolean algebra; fixed point; multiplexers; signed or unsigned instructions; comparators and parity; arguments in a0 to a7. USE NOW: the calling convention (Lecture 18) and, used without being studied in this course, the PRG32 tools, the PRG32 runtime calls, the PRG32-QT debugger. UNDERSTAND LATER: nothing. A slide without a badge is context: a story, an example, a question, an exercise.

## Lecture 13: Sequential Machines

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) describe a finite-state machine with a state diagram; (2) explain the clock and why a circuit must settle within one period; (3) tell a latch from a flip-flop and build a register. Builds on: only what Lecture 01 set up. Next: Lecture 14, Elementary Machines: Registers and Buses.

Closing thread: A register is flip-flops that sample on a clock edge: this is how the counter of Lecture 02 survived from one frame to the next, in hardware. Next: how registers exchange data.

## Lecture 14: Elementary Machines: Registers and Buses

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) explain how registers share a bus through three-state buffers; (2) use a shift register for serial transfer. Builds on: registers as flip-flops (Lecture 13). Next: Lecture 15, Memory.

Closing thread: A bus is a road that only one register may drive at a time, and a shift register turns a word into a stream of bits: the display of the kit receives its pixels this way. Next: memory.

## Lecture 15: Memory

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) compute the capacity of a memory from its address and data lines; (2) describe the interface between processor and memory during a load; (3) explain memory-mapped input/output. Builds on: little-endian byte order (Lecture 04). Next: Lecture 16, Permanent Memory.

Bridge. Since Lecture 02, lw t1, 0(t0) has read a word at an address computed from t0. Today that address is the one placed on the address bus, register plus constant. Lecture 19 calls this base plus displacement and compares it with the other addressing modes. Recall: In lw t1, 8(t0), which address goes on the address bus?

Closing thread: Every lw and sw of the course is a short dialogue on the address bus, the data bus and two control lines; a device answers on the same bus. Next: memory that survives without power, and caches.

**Learning status.** Learning status of this lecture. UNDERSTAND NOW: memories and addresses; little-endian byte order; processor and memory; memory-mapped I/O. USE NOW: the complete program, the PRG32 tools (used, not studied, in this course). UNDERSTAND LATER: nothing. A slide without a badge is context: a story, an example, a question, an exercise.

## Lecture 16: Permanent Memory

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) classify permanent memories and say where the cartridge is kept; (2) explain a cache hit and a cache miss, and locality; (3) compare the access times of disks and solid-state storage. Builds on: the von Neumann architecture (Lecture 03). Next: Lecture 17, Verm1, Part 3: A Body, Rules and States.

Closing thread: Memory is a hierarchy: small and fast near the processor, large and slow far away, and locality makes the trick work. Next: the third part of Verm1, which needs memory for a whole body.

## Lecture 24: Beyond One Core: Superscalar RISC-V, HPC, GPUs and FPGAs

Roadmap. Today's outcomes: (1) use the performance equation to say where time goes; (2) explain superscalar execution, vectors, GPUs and FPGAs as answers to it; (3) bound a parallel speed-up with Amdahl's law. Builds on: only what Lecture 01 set up. This is the last lecture of the course.

Closing thread: The loop that empties Verm1's map can be made faster in five ways, and each is a machine of its own. The question an engineer asks is not which machine is fastest, but which is sufficient.
